# Tashkent rebellion (1587)

The Tashkent Rebellion (1587) was a major armed uprising against the rule of the Shaybanid ruler Abdullah Khan II. The revolt was led by the local aristocracy of Tashkent in alliance with various Kazakh sultans.
Causes
The primary causes of the rebellion were the heavy-handed centralization policies of Abdullah Khan II and the unpopularity of his cousin, Uzbek Sultan, who had been appointed as the governor of Tashkent. The local nobility (notables and wealthy merchants) sought to restore their previous autonomy and privileges, which had been curtailed by the Bukhara administration.
Conflict and Participants
The rebellion broke out in early 1588 and quickly gained momentum, lasting for about three months. It wasn't confined to Tashkent alone; the unrest spread to neighboring cities along the Syr Darya, including Sighnaq, Sauran, Turkistan, Shahrukhiya, and Khujand.
A key feature of the rebellion was the involvement of Kazakh royalty. Mungatay Sultan and Din-Muhammad Sultan, the sons of Haqnazar Khan, joined the insurgents with their military forces. The total number of rebels is estimated to have been around 30,000.
The insurgents proclaimed Jan-Ali Sultan as their leader and Khan. Historical chronicles, such as the Sharaf-nama-yi-shahi, note that Jan-Ali was strategically chosen partly due to his striking resemblance to Baba Sultan, a late charismatic rebel leader who had fought Abdullah Khan II years earlier.
Suppression
Abdullah Khan II reacted swiftly to the threat. While the rebels managed to briefly seize control of major parts of Tashkent, the Shaybanid governor Uzbek Sultan received significant reinforcements from Bukhara. In a decisive confrontation, the professional Shaybanid army managed to break the rebel lines. Jan-Ali Sultan was killed during the suppression, and the Kazakh allies were forced to retreat back to the steppes.
